excerpt: The article reports that an Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality review and meta-analysis found MBIs compared to active controls had a mixture of only moderate, low, or no efficacy depending on the disorder. It states that efficacy was moderate for reducing symptoms of anxiety, depression, and pain; low for reducing stress and improving quality of life; and absent or insufficiently evidenced for attention, positive mood, substance abuse, eating habits, sleep, and weight control.
overview: This evidence constrains the practical interpretation of mindfulness interventions. It supports selective and condition-specific claims while undermining broad claims that mindfulness is a generally strong therapy across outcomes. The result is comparative to active controls, making it especially relevant to efficacy rather than mere demand or wait-list effects.
title: Mixed Clinical Efficacy
